headline: Wireless Android Auto drains batteries and causes connection issues
summary: Users report significant battery drain, overheating, and unreliable connections with wireless Android Auto, often requiring a cable anyway.
details: While wireless Android Auto promises a clutter-free experience, many users are finding it impractical due to excessive battery drain. On phones like the Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra and Google Pixel 10 Pro XL, the feature can deplete the battery significantly within hours, requiring frequent charging.

Beyond battery life, the high power consumption causes phones to run unusually warm. This is particularly problematic in hot climates, where the combined heat can lead to performance throttling and potentially impact long-term battery health.

Connection issues are another major frustration. Users report random disconnects, Android Auto failing to launch, and difficulties reconnecting after short stops. These problems often necessitate restarting the car's infotainment system or toggling airplane mode to restore functionality.

Call latency is also an issue, with noticeable delays impacting conversations. Minor connection hiccups can introduce lag to most actions within Android Auto, making even simple tasks like changing tracks feel unresponsive and annoying.

The experience with wireless Android Auto can be inconsistent across different devices. While some phones offer a near-flawless experience, others, like the Pixel 8 Pro, frequently disconnect, take a long time to connect, or suffer from laggy touch inputs.

Compared to wireless CarPlay, which is often described as more reliable and consistent, wireless Android Auto falls short for many. While wired Android Auto also has issues, they are typically easier to resolve by simply replugging the cable.

headline: Turn old hard drives into faster, more reliable storage with RAID
summary: RAID combines multiple disks to function as a single unit, offering faster speeds and data redundancy. Learn how to set up your own array.
details: Don't let those old hard drives gather dust! RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) can combine multiple disks to function as a single unit, giving them a new purpose. This setup can significantly boost transfer speeds and provide crucial data redundancy, making your storage more reliable.

RAID works by distributing your files across two or more disks. This striping process results in much faster read and write times compared to a single conventional HDD, though it won't match SSD speeds. Crucially, if one drive fails, you can still recover your files from the others, preventing data loss.

There are several types of RAID arrays, each with different benefits. RAID 0 stripes data across disks for maximum speed but offers no data protection – a single drive failure means losing everything. It's great for speed but terrible for safety.

For reliability, RAID 1 mirrors data across all disks in the array. If one drive fails, your data remains intact on the others. This setup is ideal for important projects but sacrifices storage space, using only 50% of the total capacity.

More complex options include RAID 5, which requires at least three drives and reconstructs data if one fails, and RAID 10, a combination of RAID 0 and RAID 1 that offers both speed and redundancy but can be vulnerable if a mirrored pair fails.

Setting up a RAID array can be done through software or hardware. Software RAID, available in operating systems like macOS (Disk Utility) and Windows (Disk Management), is easier but offers less optimal performance. Paid software like StableBit DrivePool and SnapRAID provide additional features.

For the best performance and drive protection, hardware-based RAID is recommended. This involves dedicated controllers that offer superior reliability and speed but can be more complex to set up, sometimes requiring a dedicated RAID controller card.
